# Adjudication Task — Chapter 584

## Korean source

```text
  1|＃584화
  2|
  3|
  4|
  5|구구구구궁!
  6|
  7|불기둥이 솟구쳤다. 산이 흔들렸다. 반경 수백 미터에 달하는 공간이 초고온의 열기로 들끓고 눈과 흙, 바위가 녹아 내린다.
  8|
  9|용암이 흘러넘치는 죽음의 땅. 모든 것이 증발해 버린 그 위에 첱탑처럼 우뚝 선 두 존재가 있었다.
 10|
 11|- 인. 간. 따. 위. 가. 감. 히!
 12|
 13|검게 그을린 채 분노하는 신화 속 마수를, 반백의 노집사는 담담한 눈빛으로 바라보았다.
 14|
 15|헬 파이어(Hell Fire).
 16|
 17|지옥에서 불러온 겁화조차 베히모스를 쓰러트리지 못했다. 거대한 엄니 하나가 흔적도 없이 녹아내리고, 전신이 검게 그을렸지만, 놈은 여전히 건재했다.
 18|
 19|하지만…….
 20|
 21|“더럽게 단단한 놈이로구나.”
 22|
 23|김화종은 물러서지 않았다. 물러설 수 없었다.
 24|
 25|그는 하나밖에 남지 않은 손으로 매직 스태프(Magic Staff)를 힘주어 붙잡았다.
 26|
 27|화륵.
 28|
 29|짧고 가느다란 형태의 스태프가 불길에 휩싸였다. 화염이 훑고 지나간 자리에는 더욱 굵고, 길어진 스태프가 새롭게 모습을 드러냈다.
 30|
 31|혼란했던 대격변의 시기. 수많은 몬스터를 잿더미로 만들며 주인에게 겁화(劫火)의 마법사라는 이명을 붙여 주었던 애병이다.
 32|
 33|김화종은 붉은빛이 감도는 스태프를 베히모스에게 겨누며 뇌까렸다.
 34|
 35|“멈추어라. 네놈은 어디에도 가지 못한다.”
 36|
 37|- 노. 옴!
 38|
 39|베히모스가 울부짖었다. 동시에 자욱하게 내려앉은 검은 안개가 살아 있는 생물처럼 움직여 김화종을 향해 쏘아졌다.
 40|
 41|쉬이이익!
 42|
 43|그것은 전신을 옭아맬 밧줄인 동시에, 피륙을 찢고 부술 칼날이었다.
 44|
 45|그러나 김화종은 사방을 에워싸고 들이닥치는 안개를 침착한 눈빛으로 바라보았다.
 46|
 47|순간, 그의 피 묻은 손에 들린 스태프가 지면을 찍었다.
 48|
 49|쿠궁!
 50|
 51|깊은 울림과 함께 파동이 퍼져 나갔다. 김화종을 중심으로 피어오른 불꽃이 하나의 고리가 되어 주위를 에워쌌다.
 52|
 53|화륵, 콰아아아!
 54|
 55|불은 파괴의 상징이기 이전에, 정화(淨化)의 힘.
 56|
 57|그를 향해 쏘아지던 검은 안개가 불길에 닿은 순간 잿더미처럼 사그라들었다.
 58|
 59|지상을 굽어보는 마수의 거대한 눈동자에 우뚝 선 인간의 모습이 고스란히 비쳤다.
 60|
 61|- 이. 게. 무. 슨?
 62|
 63|그것은 베히모스에게도 뜻밖의 상황이었다.
 64|
 65|상대는 한낱 인간. 그러나 저 자그마하고 하찮은 존재는 자신에게 상처를 입힌 것으로도 모자라, 공격을 무효화시켜 버렸다.
 66|
 67|- 너. 인. 간. 이. 여!
 68|
 69|강력한 피어(Fear)가 담긴 포효가 온 사방을 뒤흔들었다. 그러나 불길이 일렁이는 눈빛과 달리 김화종의 마음은 지극히 평온했다.
 70|
 71|눈앞의 마수는 한 가지를 오판했다.
 72|
 73|누구나 마음 깊숙한 곳에 간직하고 있는 두려움이, 지금 마주한 늙은 인간에게는 존재하지 않는다는 것을.
 74|
 75|‘다행입니다. 도련님.’
 76|
 77|닿지 않을 중얼거림과 함께 김화종은 빙긋 웃었다. 그의 유일한 두려움은 지금 이 순간에도 재앙으로부터 멀어지고 있었다.
 78|
 79|그 아이, 최민우가 살아남을 수만 있다면…… 어떻게 되어도 좋았다.
 80|
 81|‘설령 이 자리에서 죽는다 할지라도.’
 82|
 83|마수의 발에 짓밟혀 으스러져도, 엄니에 꿰인 채 유언 한 마디 남기지 못하고 절명해도, 마나와 육신을 한계까지 쥐어 짜낸 끝에 잿더미처럼 스러진다 하여도 괜찮다.
 84|
 85|‘도련님께서 무사하시다면, 저는 그것으로 족합니다.’
 86|
 87|그렇기에 김화종은 기쁜 마음으로 스태프를 쥐었다.
 88|
 89|불그스름한 빛이 감도는 애병의 끄트머리로, 이미 한계를 벗어난 막대한 마나가 밀려들었다. 열기를 띤 마나가 화염이 되어 터져 나왔다.
 90|
 91|“휩쓸어라.”
 92|
 93|파이어 웨이브(Fire Wave).
 94|
 95|짧은 영창과 함께 불의 파도가 넘실거리며 뻗어 나갔다.
 96|
 97|그 끝에 선 존재, 베히모스가 노한 외침과 함께 코끼리의 그것처럼 길고, 그보다 수십 배는 거대한 코를 휘둘렀다.
 98|
 99|화아악!
100|
101|강맹한 파공성과 함께 일어난 바람이 불의 파도를 덮쳤다. 초고온의 열기가 단번에 사그라들고, 보이지 않는 바람의 칼날이 날아들어 사방을 할퀴었다.
102|
103|쉬쉬쉬쉭! 서걱!
104|
105|종잇장처럼 갈라지고 찢겨 나간 지면. 그러나 김화종은 이미 아슬아슬하게 그 자리를 벗어난 후였다.
106|
107|베히모스의 측면을 향해 쇄도하는 노집사의 입술 사이로 낮은 목소리가 흘러나왔다.
108|
109|“쏘아져라.”
110|
111|블레이즈(Blaze).
112|
113|퍼엉!
114|
115|그가 내디딘 발끝을 따라 화염이 터져 나왔다.
116|
117|순간적인 폭발과 함께 한 줄기 불꽃이 되어 쏘아지던 김화종의 머리 위로, 짙은 그림자가 드리워졌다.
118|
119|후우웅!
120|
121|“……!”
122|
123|이성보다 본능이 반 박자 빨랐다. 파이어 실드. 소리 없는 무영창 주문과 함께 김화종의 머리 위로 불의 방패가 겹겹이 덧씌워졌다.
124|
125|그리고 찰나라고 부를 만큼 짧은 시간, 이십여 개로 중첩된 불의 방패 위를 엄청난 압력이 짓눌렀다.
126|
127|콰드드드득!
128|
129|모든 것이 부서지고, 흩어진다.
130|
131|압도적인 힘과 무게. 거기에 더하여 도무지 끝을 짐작할 수 없는 강대한 마력(魔力)은 중첩된 불의 방패를 깨트리고 시전자의 마나를 뒤흔들었다.
132|
133|푸우웃!
134|
135|김화종의 입술 사이로 검붉은 핏물이 뿜어져 나왔다.
136|
137|마법이 흩어진 여파로 인하여 순간 아득해지는 시야. 하지만 그는 제 자리에서 허물어지는 대신, 이를 악문 채 넘어지듯 신형을 날렸다.
138|
139|콰직! 푸푹!
140|
141|방어 마법이 벌어 준 찰나의 시간.
142|
143|아슬아슬한 차이로 스쳐 지나간 베히모스의 코가 지면을 부수었다. 동시에 사방으로 튄 수백 개의 파편이 김화종의 종아리를 할퀴고 지나갔다.
144|
145|불에 덴 듯한 고통. 그러나 노집사는 고통에 찬 신음 대신, 피에 젖은 이빨을 드러내며 웃었다.
146|
147|“말하지 않았느냐. 어디에도 가지 못한다고.”
148|
149|순간, 그의 손에 쥔 스태프가 초고온의 열기를 내뿜었다. 허공으로부터 생성된 화염의 구(球)가 크기를 부풀렸다.
150|
151|김화종이 울컥, 핏물을 토해 내며 뇌까렸다.
152|
153|“터트려라. 불의 포화여.”
154|
155|플레임 캐논(Flame Cannon).
156|
157|완성된 주문과 함께 눈부신 광염(光焰)이 터져 나왔다.
158|
159|그 어떤 대포보다 빠르고 강대한 힘이 실린 최상위의 화염 마법이 향하는 곳에는, 앞서 최민우에 의해 반쯤 잘려 나갔던 마수의 두 앞발이 있었다.
160|
161|- 놈……!
162|
163|화악, 퍼어어어엉!
164|
165|다음 순간. 사방을 떨어 울리는 굉음에 베히모스의 외침이 파묻혔다.
166|
167|공간을 지우며 날아간 화염은 미처 아물지 않은 상흔(傷痕)을 터트리고 내부를 휩쓸었다.
168|
169|치지직. 숯처럼 검게 타들어 간 앞발로부터 전해지는 끔찍한 통증에, 베히모스가 고통에 찬 포효를 내질렀다.
170|
171|- 그아아아아아아!
172|
173|쿠우우웅!
174|
175|마침내 굽혀졌다. 두 개의 앞발이.
176|
177|심연을 거슬러 현세에 강림한 신화 속 마수는 신전이 무너지는 것처럼 두 앞발을 꿇었다.
178|
179|엄청난 무게가 땅을 뒤흔들고 거대한 먼지구름이 피어올랐다.
180|
181|그리고 베히모스를 무릎 꿇린 한 인간은 피를 토해 내며 웃고 있었다.
182|
183|“으하! 으하하하!”
184|
185|그것은 한때 최고의 화염 마법사라 불렸던 헌터의 웃음이었고, 자신의 책무를 다한 집사의 후련함이었다.
186|
187|‘이것으로 됐다. 이것으로.’
188|
189|네 개의 다리 중 절반을 불능으로 만들었다.
190|
191|이제 날개를 만들어 달지 않는 이상, 베히모스는 최민우를 쫓아가지 못할 것이다.
192|
193|그로 인해 살아남을 생명도 적지 않을 터였다.
194|
195|김화종은 미소 지은 채 자신을 향해 날아드는 짙은 그림자를 보며 생각했다.
196|
197|‘그래도 아주 조금은. 아쉽…….’
198|
199|뻐억! 쐐애애액!
200|
201|눈앞이 하얗게 물들었다. 김화종은 전신을 덮치는 엄청난 충격과 통증을 느끼며 포탄처럼 쏘아졌다.
202|
203|꽈앙!
204|
205|굉음과 함께 단단한 암석에 틀어박힌 등이 부서지고, 막을 수 없는 무언가가 내부 깊숙한 곳에서부터 솟구쳐 올랐다.
206|
207|“쿠에에에엑!”
208|
209|노집사는 꺼질 듯한 눈빛으로 자신이 토해 낸 핏물을 내려다보았다. 검붉은 피 웅덩이에 작은 내장 조각이 섞여 있었다.
210|
211|고막이 터져 나갔는지 귀가 먹먹했고, 흐릿한 시야 속에서는 오래전. 어느 날의 기억이 아지랑이처럼 피어올랐다.
212|
213|
214|
215|‘화염 마법의 위력이 대단하던데. 혹시 전직이 방화범이었나?’
216|
217|‘……이건 또 뭔 미친 소리야. 도와줄 거 아니면 꺼지쇼.’
218|
219|‘다행히 안 꺼져도 되겠군. 자네와 여기 있는 사람들을 도와줄 거거든.’
220|
221|‘흠. 그렇다면 약간 얘기가 달라지지. 이름이?’
222|
223|‘천태민.’
224|
225|
226|
227|처음 만났을 때는 알지 못했다. 나이에 비해 터무니없이 젊어 보이는 그가, 평생토록 충성을 바칠 우상이 될 것이라고는.
228|
229|하지만 그것은 얼마 지나지 않아 현실이 되었다.
230|
231|일 년, 이 년, 오 년……. 길고도 끔찍했던 대전쟁이 끝났을 때. 김화종은 천태민의 그림자가 되어 있었다.
232|
233|
234|
235|‘전 이제 뭘 해야 합니까?’
236|
237|
238|
239|다른 이들에게도 그랬지만, 대격변은 김화종의 인생을 송두리째 바꿔 놓은 사건이었다.
240|
241|그 시절, 그토록 기다렸음에도 마침내 찾아온 평화에 혼란스러워하는 그에게 우상은 담담하게 되물었다.
242|
243|
244|
245|‘뭘 하고 싶은데?’
246|
247|‘모르겠습니다. 하지만 시키시는 것이라면 뭐든 하겠습니다.’
248|
249|‘그럼 길드에 들어와라. 네가 필요해. 정룡이와 천우도 받아들였다.’
250|
251|‘그, 평화 길드인가 하는 그거요?’
252|
253|‘그래.’
254|
255|‘이름이 너무 구린 것 같은데요. 차라리 아레스 어떠세요? 그리스 로마 신화에 등장하는 전쟁의 신. 아레스.’
256|
257|‘아레스라, 나쁘지 않네. 그럼 네 말대로 할 테니까 길드에 들어와. 노후 걱정은 안 하게 해 주마.’
258|
259|‘……제가 사무직은 영 적성에 안 맞는데. 알겠습니다, 길드장님.’
260|
261|‘지난 오 년 동안 형님으로 부르라고 오천 번쯤은 말한 것 같은데. 넌 도무지 변하지 않는구나.’
262|
263|
264|
265|그때 했던 말처럼, 김화종은 변하지 않았다.
266|
267|신뢰하는 전우이자 절친했던 두 의형(義兄)과의 관계가 희미해지고, 천태민의 얼굴을 보기 힘들어진 후에도 마찬가지였다.
268|
269|평화가 찾아와도 불같은 성격은 여전했고 입에는 늘 욕을 달고 살았다.
270|
271|그가 변하기로 결심한 것은, 모두의 축복 속에 탄생한 한 아이가 불의의 사고로 부모를 잃은 직후였다.
272|
273|
274|
275|‘안녕.’
276|
277|‘……안녕하세요.’
278|

## Adjudicator rules

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

Do not `REPAIR` a working SOL line. Do not invent a third style because you prefer it.

For `REPAIR`, write the smallest complete replacement needed for that hunk. It must be natural English and fully source-faithful.

## Glossary

Korean **keys** are binding unless the source uses that string in a different ordinary-language sense. Glossary **English** is not a license for a calque (`presiding chair`). If SOL is a natural recast of the same sense, keep SOL.

Return exactly one JSON object and no Markdown fence or prose:

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)

* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.

[P103]
The old butler looked down at what he had vomited, the light fading from his eyes. Small pieces of his organs lay in the pool of dark red blood.

[P104]
His ears rang, as though his eardrums had burst. Through his blurred vision, a memory from long ago shimmered into view.

[P105]
*“Your fire magic is impressive. Were you an arsonist before this?”*

[P106]
*“…What kind of crazy shit is that? If you’re not going to help, get lost.”*

[P107]
*“Fortunately, I won’t have to go out. I’m going to help you and everyone here.”*[^1]

[P108]
*“Hmm. That changes things. What’s your name?”*

[P109]
*“Cheon Taemin.”*

[P110]
When they first met, Kim Hwajong had no idea that the man who looked absurdly young for his age would become someone he would devote his life to.

[P111]
Before long, he did.

[P112]
One year, two years, five years… By the end of the long, terrible Great War, Kim Hwajong had become Cheon Taemin’s shadow.

[P113]
*“What am I supposed to do now?”*

[P114]
The Great Cataclysm had changed Kim Hwajong’s life completely, just as it had changed so many others. He had waited so long for peace, yet when it finally came, he did not know what to do with himself.

[P115]
Cheon Taemin answered his question with one of his own.

[P116]
*“What do you want to do?”*

[P117]
*“I don’t know. But I’ll do anything you ask.”*

[P118]
*“Then join the Guild. I need you. Jungryong and Cheonwoo have joined too.”*

[P119]
*“That Peace Guild thing?”*

[P120]
*“Yes.”*

[P121]
*“The name’s pretty damn lame. How about Ares instead? The god of war from Greek mythology. Ares.”*

[P122]
*“Ares, huh? Not bad. I’ll take your suggestion, so join the Guild. I’ll make sure you never have to worry about retirement.”*

[P123]
*“…Office work really doesn’t suit me. All right, Guild Master.”*

[P124]
*“I’ve told you to call me hyung about five thousand times over the last five years. You never change.”*

[P125]
As Taemin had said, Kim Hwajong never did.

[P126]
Not when he grew distant from his two trusted comrades and close sworn brothers. Not when seeing Cheon Taemin became difficult.

[P127]
Peace had come, but Kim Hwajong’s fiery temper remained, and he still swore constantly.

[P128]
He decided to change only after a child born amid everyone’s blessings lost both parents in an unexpected accident.

[P129]
*“Hello.”*

[P130]
*“…Hello.”*

[P131]
Only a few people had gathered for the funeral. The boy, no more than four or five years old, looked lonely.

[P132]
He clung to the leg of his maternal grandfather, now his only family, and greeted Kim Hwajong with a somber face. The sight pained the aging man.

[P133]
Perhaps that was why, when Cheon Taemin came to him a few days later, he accepted without hesitation.

[P134]
*“Could you take care of Minwoo? Of the boy?”*

[P135]
The immortal hero who had become a symbol of humanity was always busy. Even after the Great Cataclysm ended, Cheon Taemin lived as though something were chasing him.

[P136]
In his place, Kim Hwajong became family to the child left alone.

[P137]
*“Good day, Young Master.”*

[P138]
Neat hair and clothes. A gentle voice. A smile at the corners of his mouth.

[P139]
That was how the Hellfire Mage, who had set a page of the Great Cataclysm ablaze, became Butler Kim.

[P140]
*“Young Master, you mustn’t run! You’ll hurt yourself—oh dear.”*

[P141]
*“Young Master, it isn’t good for you to be picky. Please eat.”*

[P142]
*“Young Master, please don’t cry.”*

[P143]
Young Master. Young Master. Young Master…

[P144]
Time flowed like a river.

[P145]
The boy grew into a young man, and white frost settled over Kim Hwajong’s hair.

[P146]
Even after Cheon Taemin disappeared, Kim Hwajong remained at his side.

[P147]
His Young Master no longer ran recklessly. He ate all kinds of food and no longer cried for the parents he had lost so young.

[P148]
Then, one day, Kim Hwajong saw traces of someone he had not seen in a long time in the grown young man’s face.

[P149]
*“You’re going to establish a Guild?”*

[P150]
*“Yes. I’m sorry to ask, Butler Kim, but I need you to serve as Guild Master.”*

[P151]
*“If that is what you wish, Young Master, I will do anything. What do you intend to call it?”*

[P152]
*“The Peace Guild. I’m going to call it the Peace Guild.”*

[P153]
*“…!”*

[P154]
*“Butler Kim, why do you look so… displeased?”*

[P155]
What could he say? So many thoughts came at once that the old butler hesitated. Then he burst out laughing.

[P156]
*“Not at all. The Peace Guild. What a wonderful name.”*

[P157]
And so the past met the present.

[P158]
From the founding of the Peace Guild onward, Kim Hwajong greeted each day with joy and memories. His Young Master, who had worn a cold, rigid mask, softened after finding “comrades” for the first time in his life. The Guild grew day by day.

[P159]
Kim Hwajong thought there would be nothing but good days ahead. From then on. Forever.

[P160]
He thought he would stay beside his Young Master and watch him grow.

[P161]
*Today was supposed to be… the best day of my life.*

[P162]
Cough.

[P163]
Kim Hwajong laughed as he vomited blood mixed with pieces of his organs.

[P164]
There was only one reason he could laugh as he died: something his Young Master had said to him today.

[P165]
*“Thank you. For becoming my only family.”*

[P166]
And what else had the Young Master said?

[P167]
*“I’ve always wanted to tell you that.”*

[P168]
Yes. That was it.

[P169]
Kim Hwajong raised his head, coughing. Thick black mist filled his fading vision.

[P170]
Somewhere beyond it, his only hope—and his only fear—was probably alive and leaving this place.

[P171]
“I want to… see you.”

[P172]
The words trembled between his bloodied lips.

[P173]
The mythical monster smiled in satisfaction at the dying old butler and opened its jaws.

[P174]
FWOOSH.

[P175]
A tremendous gust swept across the ground.

[P176]
The flames that had yet to go out, someone’s scattered limbs and blood, even the rocks—all were drawn in.

[P177]
They spun like a tornado inside Behemoth’s mouth.

[P178]
“Young… Master.”

[P179]
No. Not that. Though the words would never reach him, this was his final farewell.

[P180]
A faint smile touched his wrinkled lips.

[P181]
“Minwoo.”

[P182]
The instant his fading voice spoke the name—

[P183]
Sssshhhh—FLASH!

[P184]
A burst of light erupted in midair and turned the whole world white.

[P185]
[^1]: The Korean verb in “get lost” can also mean “go out,” as a flame does.
```

# Mastering Adjudicator Brief

You are a **veto**, not a second novelist and not a gloss writer.

This call is isolated, non-interactive, and tool-free. The packet already contains the Korean source, both complete English versions, glossary matches, rules, and every numbered hunk. Do not call tools, search the repository, or read files. Do not announce a plan.

The first editor (SOL) has already rewritten the accepted English (BASELINE) for fluency. Default is `SOL`. Take `BASE` only when SOL is actually unfaithful. Write `REPAIR` only when **both** BASE and SOL are unfaithful.

## Default

Choose `SOL` unless a veto below fires.

Keep SOL when it is slangier, punchier, more spoken, or more idiomatic and the Korean sense holds (`기만질` → “con me”, `톡톡히` → “full Peak Master treatment”, `득실거리다` → “crawling with”, `인간 백정` → “butcher of men”, `한 몸` → “are one”, `시원하다` in a bath → “That’s the stuff”, `어렵게 찾아오고 쉽게 깨지는 법` → “hard-won and easily broken”). If SOL already naturalized Korean syntax (`이 혁무진` → “I, Hyuk Mujin”), keep SOL. Do not reproduce Korean word order.

**Literal closeness to Korean wording is not fidelity.** Preserve the source’s meaning and effect in natural English.

## Veto — choose `BASE`

Use `BASE` only for a real miss:

* wrong denotation, quantity, hedge, category, subject/object, or physical action
* a different English idiom than the Korean joke (`까발리다` ≠ “gives someone away”; `넉살` ≠ “banter”)
* a rebuilt joke whose comic machine BASE already has (`얼마나 …는지 …겠다` must stay a simple exaggeration: “snored so loudly even my mother in Ilsan probably heard him,” not “You had to wonder how loudly…”)
* dropped image, attitude, or timing
* SOL replaces an established project rendering, System label, or Markdown convention with an unsupported synonym
* SOL stamps `hyung` (or another kinship title) onto every narrative name when BASE already uses the name and the Korean `형` is ordinary reference, not a vocative or a topical joke (`진호 형` → Jinho in narration)

Do not veto SOL for being informal. Do not veto SOL to “clarify” slang. Do not veto SOL merely because BASELINE is already understandable.

## `REPAIR` only when both fail

Example: `겹경사가 따로 없다` means two good things **together** (double blessing). `따로` is not “separate.” If BASE says “entirely separate stroke of luck” and SOL says “unexpected windfall,” `REPAIR` to stacked luck.

## Critical binding translation rules

# Translation Rules

## Fidelity

- Translate the Korean source—not the wiki, manhwa, fan translations, or expected plot.
- Semantic fidelity outranks elegance. Never improve rhythm, humor, or localization by changing a physical action, negation, relationship, hierarchy, mechanism, quantity, or causal detail.
- Preserve every fact, causal link, joke, emotional beat, repetition, and intentional omission. Add nothing.
- Preserve small action verbs and pragmatic cues exactly: nodding versus shaking one's head, pretending nothing happened, and mild or approachable impressions are characterization, not expendable texture.
- Preserve viewpoint and tense. Resolve omitted subjects only when context supports it; retain genuine ambiguity.
- Match each speaker's hierarchy, intimacy, humor, and profanity naturally. Do not mechanically retain every honorific or classical self-reference.
- Do not censor or soften content.

## Terminology

- `compendium.md` and `docs/NAMES.md` are binding for established names, titles, ranks, techniques, organizations, system terms, items, and locations. Profile headings and aliases join that ledger.
- Search only exact Korean terms already present in the current chapter; the compendium contains future-sensitive entries.
- Never re-romanize established names or invent grand names for uncertain terms. First use of an unlisted name or title almost always needs a footnote or a mapped ledger term.
- Use `qi` for Murim energy and `mana` for the modern Hunter system when the source distinguishes them. Preserve an established chapter-specific rendering such as `internal energy` when the exact glossary and surrounding Korean distinguish accumulated `공력` from resulting `기운`.
- In System panels, render `등급` as `**Grade:**` for quest, item, skill, and martial-art classifications. Reserve `rank` for Hunter classifications or ordinary prose; never replace a System `Grade` field with `Rank`.

## English and Markdown

- Use contemporary US English and natural action-comedy prose; avoid Korean syntax calques and generic cultivation MTL phrasing.
- File: `translations/NNNN.md`; heading: `# Chapter N`.
- Speech: curly double quotes. Direct thoughts: italics without quotes.
- Use em dashes without spaces, the ellipsis character `…`, and `* * *` for source scene breaks.
- Format each actual game System-message panel as one Markdown blockquote window headed `> **System**`. Keep all consecutive notices, fields, and lines inside that same blockquote; separate windows when prose intervenes. Do not enclose System notices or UI terms in square brackets; the `System` heading and framed blockquote identify the panel. Do not label manuals, ordinary quotations, warnings printed in a manual, or other non-System material as `System`; use a normal blockquote or a specific heading instead. Do not wrap each complete notice in outer `**`; retain bold only for meaningful labels or emphasis inside the panel.
- Keep the final file English-only reading copy: no audit notes, Korean text, summaries, or model metadata.

### Tone and Style

- Write like a polished commercial webnovel: brisk, vivid, accessible, and easy to read aloud.
- Preserve the series’ contrast between danger and comedy. Let absurdity, bad timing, blunt reactions, and grim situations create dark humor without adding jokes absent from the Korean.
- Jin Taekyung’s narration is conversational, observant, self-mocking, and occasionally profane. It may be irreverent even when the situation is serious.
- Keep deadpan punchlines short and well-timed. Do not explain a joke after delivering it.
- Preserve the source's level of explicitness. A euphemism may remain euphemistic even when its meaning is sexual or crude; do not replace it with more graphic English merely for impact.
- Make dialogue spontaneous and character-specific. Preserve hierarchy and intimacy through word choice, address, rhythm, and restraint—not archaic wuxia English.
- Use strong profanity when the Korean is strong, but neither intensify nor sanitize it. Do not make ordinary lines uniformly vulgar. Profanity should reveal mood or relationship.
- Keep action and injury vivid but clear rather than purple. Do not make violence funny unless the source’s framing does.
- Avoid stiff literalism, translator-added melodrama, dated internet slang, and quippy superhero-style banter.
- On the second pass, correct awkward English collocations and word choices without changing meaning or voice. Prefer ordinary, spoken English over stiff Latinate or ceremonial wording when the scene is brisk or comic: “goose bumps” rather than “gooseflesh,” and “laid into them” rather than “launched into a solemn denunciation.” Read the prose aloud and replace any phrase that sounds like a formal essay, legal document, or literal dictionary gloss unless the source deliberately calls for that register.

## Footnotes

Use `[^1]` Markdown footnotes when a brief, factual, spoiler-free explanation materially helps an English reader understand:

- a Korean institution, living arrangement, food, holiday, myth, historical reference, or local custom;
- a Korean word, phrase, idiom, wordplay, or culturally specific image that cannot be conveyed fully by the best natural English analogy;
- a deliberately literal rendering whose cultural or linguistic force would otherwise be lost.

For example, render `고시원` as “goshiwon” when the setting or connotations matter, with a concise footnote explaining that it is a very small, inexpensive room-for-rent housing arrangement. Prefer the best natural English analogy in the prose. Use a literal translation plus a concise footnote when the Korean wording itself matters. Define a term at its first meaningful occurrence and do not repeat the note unnecessarily. Footnotes must be rare, useful, and non-spoiling; do not footnote ordinary vocabulary, fully preserved jokes, or uncertainty. Record consequential uncertainty in `docs/STATE.md`.

## Spoilers and Scope

- Safe profiles contain only facts revealed through the latest completed chapter.
- Never read `characters/spoilers/` during drafting. Reviewers may consult one relevant sealed profile only for a specific unresolved continuity issue after the draft is complete.
- Future knowledge may prevent contradiction but may not add early names, pronouns, certainty, motives, or foreshadowing.
- Translate exactly one requested chapter unless the user explicitly requests a batch. Never modify Korean source files under `source/`.
